blocks.text: “I was lucky to be alive when things were happening,” says James Barnor. Accra on the eve of independence, London in the days of the Beatles: reason enough to call himself Lucky Jim. A lucky man, in short ( Lucky Jim is also a Kingsley Amis novel, published in 1954, different era, same vein). At 97, he headlines an opening that doubles as a housewarming.

At 51, rue Saint-Louis-en-l’Île, Galerie Clémentine de la Féronnière reopens after several weeks of work. More than 250 m² (about 2,700 square feet) of exhibition space extending from the street-front bookshop, a showroom, an office dedicated to digitizing and consulting photographic collections: the back room has taken on the air of an archive reading room. The choice of guest was obvious. Since 2015, the team has worked on James Barnor’s archive, sorted and catalogued with him on site between 2017 and 2021. A long-haul loyalty.

There is a certain delight in finding James Barnor in his own pictures, the man who spent his life composing other people’s. Accra, 1952: a young father dressed all in white, straight as a rod against a whitewashed wall, he holds his son Daniel in his christening gown. That same year, on assignment for the Daily Graphic , he leans over a staircase banister, twin-lens camera in hand and saucer flash at the ready, a friend with a cigarette on his lips playing prompter. Dressed to the nines, already.

Then England. James Barnor landed in Liverpool on December 1, 1959, and worked night shifts in a factory alongside a Ghanaian boxer, Attuquaye Clottey, who thought he was mad to have left his studio. In 1960 came Dennis Kemp, a lecturer for Kodak: “Look I can offer you board and lodging but no pay,” he told him (Barnor recalled it in 2019). His friend photographed him draped in his kente, leaning on an “England” road sign in Shropshire, motorbike parked in the hedge, or seated beneath a giant “CAFÉ” sign. The ease of a prince on tour.

Back in Accra in the late 1960s, James Barnor was hired by Agfa-Gevaert to set up the country’s first color lab. There he posed an assistant among bottles of developing chemicals, pink, green, white, coral, in place of a color chart. A makeshift swatch book, mischief intact. Elsewhere, a grid of 12 frames shot at the Agfa-Gevaert laboratory in Mortsel, Belgium: he slips in beside a model in a striped top, then takes the colored backdrop alone. Self-portrait as a diligent student.

On October 22, the Fondation Cartier pour l’art contemporain opens “Le temps des récoltes” (The Time of Harvests) by Ibrahim Mahama, which includes the “Agip” series, made for the brand’s 1974 calendar. The occasion for James Barnor’s return to Paris. “I’m lucky to be alive and to be telling the story about my work,” he says. Lucky Jim, still.
James Barnor, “Lucky Jim” is on view through November 21, 2026 at Galerie Clémentine de la Féronnière , Paris.
